A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code , and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.

Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse , and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse.

Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence

Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.

When we introduced Muse Spark , we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.

The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

For more details about our evaluations, see our report .

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.

We call this Active Memory : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

items.title: Living in the Weimar era of Ruby
items.summary: ruby, vibecoding
items.content:
Much has been said about the DHH keynote that he gave at RailsWorld. To me, it was the voice of a person in an existential crisis, but also a very jaded one. “Look how I don’t care anymore, and you should not care either” is not a great message when you are the headline speaker at the conference - let’s call it CareConf - that you have, yourself, lobbied for.

The message from the supreme leader was clear: we vibe-rewrote HEY in a more performant way, it worked great, we neither need nor care about Rails anymore. I honestly believe that, instead of amassing even more applause via vitriolic truth-bombing, he could have just left the toy he no longer loves - including its community - in peace.

But here is the thing: the rich and famous losing interest in the good stuff does not oblige the rest of us to. If anything, it frees up the room.

🧭 I am currently available for contract work.

Hire me to help make your Rails app better!

I must admit that for a few days I felt very depressed about it all. Not about “AIs writing all the code” - that much is clear to me, and I do not lament the changing landscape of the craft - I do lament the landscape of usage , which is a topic for another article. It is abundantly clear that the LLMs are here to stay, that typing every single line by hand is no longer sustainable, and that the scales have shifted profoundly. What made me depressed was just how little care there was about the Ruby ecosystem and community, and the disdain with which David flushed the entire Rails and Ruby culture down the drain for the sake of “running it on a single Raspberry Pi”, as he put it.

What I am actually observing is something different: a renaissance, even though quite a few prominent Rubyists have moved on to other stacks - which are now much more open to exploration, as you don’t have to write all that… gunk - let’s call it what it is - by hand. A detailed unpack of 7 little-endian integers is not particularly interesting, nor artistic - it’s just gunk, and I won’t miss it. Unless struct packing is needed to make it fast, but then we can always art-direct additionally.

There was an interesting time in German history, right between the two World Wars - the “interbellum”, the time of the Weimar Republic. It was very turbulent, and a lot of it wasn’t pretty in the slightest - social difficulties, unemployment, incredible inflation, squalid living conditions, the emergence of the wildest movements, cabarets and cults imaginable… but there was also something else. The “Roaring Twenties” of Weimar Germany also produced an incredible number of great, whimsical, fascinating artistic movements. From the Bauhaus to the Berlin gay cabarets, from Kurt Weill to Fritz Lang’s Metropolis - it was a booming time, and a lot of what appeared then is still valued and cherished today.

And it was a technological boom as well - the ever more widespread use of electricity, the large-scale deployment of modern pharmaceuticals, the subways, the automobile… fascinating times.

I know how that era ended, and no - that is not the part of the analogy I am after. The part I am after is this: the old order had lost interest, nobody was in charge, the ground was shifting under everybody’s feet - and that is precisely when the most interesting work got made. Great turmoil, great industrial change, no adult supervision. Sound familiar?

And the Ruby community has always been artistic, as early as the work of _why. Aesthetics were, after all, what drew a lot of people into Rails. The fact that you didn’t need the parentheses. The fact that thingswerenotwritteninoneword as if invented by a Dutchman, that there was no “this is an attribute and this is a method” confusion… a lot of things about the language were just aesthetically brilliant.

And with the abundance of new tooling, the right mindset to look at the state of the ecosystem is this:

You are right but it also feels short-sighted? You have the most powerful tool you ever had, you…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
items.content:
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.

A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.

If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.

items.content:
CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2)

Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on.

Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session:

For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap .

If it stays on by default, please at least:

Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually).

With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon.

Related: #40969 , #41188 , #46468 , #48050 , #42457 , #37537

@Yihua-Liu-1997 thanks for reporting this, I hit it myself... stuff should not be creating mystery servers and processes all of a sudden on small version number bumps without giving people a heads-up...

agreed. the CLI is unusable until this is fixed.

I can confirm this on Windows 10 LTSC with Codex CLI 0.157.0

Setting daemon_auto_start = false in config.toml resolves the issue

This would preserve the security restrictions without disrupting the normal CLI workflow.

@tagorr Indeed — both 1 and 2 would work~

codex: disable daemon auto-start by default

The Codex CLI is unusable due to this bug on Windows.

This is terrible. I can't input anything on the CLI at all. You should fix this problem as soon as possible and give us 100 banked reset!

There is a useful provenance boundary behind this request:

installed CLI identity != daemon execution identity

Once the CLI copies itself into a managed release directory and a background updater can replace that copy, the process that services a later turn is no longer necessarily the artifact the user explicitly installed or invoked.

I would make the daemon expose a small execution receipt for each client attachment containing at least:

client_cli_version + daemon_binary_digest + daemon_generation + updater_state + inherited_environment_generation

A strong regression would start the daemon under environment A, attach from environment B, update the installed CLI, and verify that the client can see exactly which daemon generation/binary/environment is authoritative for the turn rather than inferring it from the foreground CLI version.

Related runtime behavioral-integrity work: https://github.com/AETHERXGLOBAL/execsurface

The part in the docs about wanting full read/write access to the entire host filesystem is why I'm running codex-cli in a hardened Raspberry Pi and ssh'ing into it.

So codex is a virus at this point? Won't be surprised if they use it to create a botnet of those sweet residential IPs for web scrapping

Start it in one directory and set some env var (I use direnv and envrc files). Then start it in another directory with different values for the same env vars. If you ask the agent to do anything with those env vars, it uses the ones from the first directory. This breaks workflows that use common env var names (GH_TOKEN, etc).

items.title: Linus Torvalds Working On A Hefty Linux Kernel Improvement With Claude Code
items.summary: linux, vibecoding
items.content:
Linus Torvalds Working On A Hefty Linux Kernel Improvement With Claude Code

Written by Michael Larabel in Linux Kernel on 11 October 2026 at 08:16 PM EDT. 48 Comments

Linux creator Linus Torvalds has been known to use AI to help with kernel debugging and outside of the kernel tree has also done some vibe coding with Google's Antigravity . He has previously said he views AI as a useful tool . It turns out he's even now using Claude Code for working on new Linux kernel features.

While waiting for the Linux 7.3-rc7 kernel release and refreshing his torvalds/linux.git repository, I was surprised to find a new kernel branch appear. Typically Torvalds isn't doing much work on branches in his main repository and typically just hosting the master branch.

The new branch to appear is noref-filemap-read-with-llm and as implied by the "LLM" postfix, is some new kernel improvements he's been working on with the help of AI / LLMs. Claude Code in particular. The branched code is working on adapting the memory management code to read from the page cache without folio references.

The code is working on addressing a Linux issue of small reads of one file from many threads contend on the folio reference counting. So the goal of the branch / patch series is to read from the page cache without folio references.

For those passionate about AI for loving or hating it, in the main patch message Linus Torvalds confirmed his AI use in creating this work and related testing and even the initial draft of the cover letter:

"The code, the test programs, the review behind the list above and the first draft of this text were done with an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under my direction. The measurements were run on my machine."

And for the impact on this situation of addressing the bottleneck of small reads of one file from many threads, the impact of the series is significant:

Quite a difference. The patches are currently on Torvalds' noref-filemap-read-with-llm Git branch . We'll see if he merges his branch for the upcoming Linux 7.4 merge window.

items.content:
Intermarche was one of the groups affected — Gabriel BOUYS / AFP

Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.

Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented".

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality".

At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.

Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.

BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores".

Those branches that were affected will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP.

Specialist French retail sector news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this.

E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores".

A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.

Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates".

It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware". It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected.

A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cyber security agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor".

"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread", the source added.

The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since Sunday night.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he wrote on X.

He added that the company's teams were "fully mobilised" to restore the situation as quickly as possible.

"An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack," he added.

The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires", the prosecutor's office said.

Intermarche condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures.

BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products".

The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks.

items.title: Valve Publishes Steam Frame CAD Files for DIY Accessories and Tweaks
items.content:
Valve Publishes Steam Frame CAD Files for DIY Accessories and Tweaks

Valve has finally released the CAD files for its Steam Frame VR headset and VR controllers, officially allowing modders and creators to create and publish their own Steam Frame accessories—as long as they're published under the correct Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial Share Alike 4.0 International license. The CAD files are published on GitLab, and they include both 3D models and technical drawings and documentation for reference when designing accessories.

The CAD files also include documentation on the electronics of the Steam Frame, including an example project documenting a USB 3.0 expansion port that could be adapted for other electronics projects. While Valve hasn't granted a sweeping explicit license to create commercial projects for the Steam Frame, it notes on the Frame's GitLab repo that "if you wish to pursue a commercial license please reach out to us at steamframecompatible at valvesoftware com," ostensibly opening the door for licensing partnerships.

(Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers
items.summary: cryptography
items.content:
(Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers

Publishing “Cryptographic Right Answers” for developers is a tradition by now. Colin Percival started in 2009 , Thomas Ptacek followed up in 2015 , and then Latacora carried on in 2018 and 2024 .

It might feel too soon for an update, but so much has changed . The timeline of the post-quantum transition dramatically shifted in early 2026 , and there is now consensus that it needs to complete by 2029. 2029! We have three years!

The good news is that, despite what you might have heard, symmetric cryptography is going to be fine, because Grover does not matter . The bad news is that all asymmetric answers changed compared to 2018 and most even compared to 2024.

The answers below assume you are not constrained by any specific compliance regime, although they are mostly compatible with FIPS 140. 1 If you need to follow something stricter like CNSA 2.0, you’ll know. Just substitute as appropriate.

Finally, remember the other big change of 2026: LLMs are very good at finding bugs now. “Get a review from the best model you can afford” is now firmly a Cryptographic Right Answer, along with the long-time classic “use a memory-safe language.”

If you’re in a rush, here’s the cheat sheet:

Encrypting data : If you’re in the cloud, KMS. Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128.

Symmetric key length : Don’t stress it. 256-bit keys if you need to pick.

Hash algorithm : SHA-2 is still fine, but use a real multihash (SequenceHash) if needed.

Random IDs : 32 random bytes, a.k.a. 256-bit random numbers.

Password handling : Argon2id or scrypt. But have you considered passkeys instead?

Key exchange : X25519+ML-KEM-768 in a secure, standard protocol.

Asymmetric encryption : HPKE with (MLKEM768-X25519 a.k.a. X-Wing, HKDF-SHA256, AES-128-GCM), or age with PQ keys.

Website or client-server application security : If you’re in the cloud, use its ALB/NLB. Otherwise, rustls, Go’s crypto/tls, BoringSSL, AWS-LC, or s2n-tls with a popular, updated ACME client.

Online backups : restic with a long random password.

If you’re in the cloud, KMS . Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128 .

Ptacek, 2015 : NaCl/libsodium default, or ChaCha20Poly1305, or AES-GCM.

Latacora, 2018 : KMS, or XSalsa20+Poly1305.

Latacora, 2024 : KMS, or NaCl’s secretbox, or XChaCha20Poly1305.

Latacora’s reasoning for why and when you’d use your cloud’s KMS is still solid, so start there.

If you’re encrypting locally, you want an AEAD where you can avoid worrying about tracking nonces or how many messages you encrypted, so you want random nonces of at least 128 bits. 2

NaCl/libsodium’s secretbox is just a paper-thin wrapper around a less common AE construction (XSalsa20+Poly1305), so instead I recommend XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305. The former is an efficient composition of a standard KDF and AES-GCM, packaged as an extended-nonce AEAD, so even if your library doesn’t provide it under that name you can assemble it from the KDF and AES-GCM APIs. 3

Regular AES-GCM and ChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces are only ok if you know for certain you won’t encrypt more than a billion messages with one key. AES-GCM-SIV is also a good AEAD choice if you happen to have it everywhere you need it, but that’s kinda unlikely. Some even newer options have nice properties like key commitment, but are not commonly available yet.

Since you have an AEAD, consider putting context in the additional data, like the user ID you’re encrypting for, or the version of the protocol. Anything not secret that you will definitely still know at decrypt time.

Very important is how you handle large messages, which KMS will not solve for you. Do not pass one large message to an AEAD, or you might be forced to process or store the plaintext before having authenticated it at decrypt time.…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

items.title: 'Unprecedented' Cyberattack cripples supermarket fridges across Europe as hackers activate automatic defrosting  — delivery and store prices also impacted by incident
items.content:
An ongoing cyberattack has reportedly struck major supermarket chains across Europe, disrupting refrigeration control systems. The attack — which has reportedly seen units set to continuously defrost at 50 degrees Celsius — is also apparently affecting deliveries and in-store pricing powered by electronic shelf labels, La Dépêche reports .

According to the report, "several" major retailers have been targeted by a cyberattack, which has hit Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French supermarkets Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Indeed, the latter's president, Dominique Schelcher, has confirmed as of Monday morning that "A cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration production facilities of several stores in our network since last night." Schelcher said teams had been mobilized to fix the issue and promised an investigation into the incident, which he described as "extremely serious."

Je confirme qu’une cyberattaque touche depuis cette nuit les installations de production de froid de plusieurs magasins de notre réseau @CooperativeU.

Nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées, en lien avec les frigoristes, pour rétablir la situation au plus vite. Une enquête devra permettre de faire toute la lumière sur cette attaque.

S’attaquer à des équipements essentiels à la conservation des produits frais et à l’approvisionnement alimentaire des Français est d’une extrême gravité et est inédit. C’est inacceptable. October 12, 2026

The report states the units have had their automatic defrosting systems activate, but that hackers have also configured the function — which normally runs for just two hours a day — into a continuous, forced defrosting cycle with the temperature set to a toasty 50 degrees Celsius. Sources reportedly described "a wave of heat" escaping from fridges and freezers

Early reports indicate losses are already approaching 300,000 euros, but could run into several million euros nationwide. Separately, NOS in the Netherlands reports that several supermarket chains have been hit with a malfunction due to a cybersecurity incident on Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall have had their websites taken down, impacting deliveries. Electronic shelf labels have also been compromised, disrupting in-store pricing. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems," Albert Heijn said in a statement.

It is unclear at this stage whether the two attacks are related or how widespread either of them is. Belgium's Delhaize chain, which belongs to Albert Heijn, has also reported disruption. Images online show stores in Amsterdam warning customers about price problems, and the suspension of loyalty programs that have also been impacted by the incident.

items.title: 'AI' is Not a Tool
items.summary: vibecoding
items.content:
(I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more)

First order of business - is ' tool ' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"?

We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later).

a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function

an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work

What I like best - A tool is something you wield .

wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control

Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use

Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc

Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events

Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try").

Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc.

What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself.

As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools.

Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation .

automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control.

A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code.

You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback.

What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right incantations. You are only a software update from everything you've 'learned' being rendered obsolete by the latest algorithm. (A soggy cold burger from which the onions have been removed) You have traded working with the world to working for a capricious robot.

It is a mistake to be haphazard about "tools" being equivalent to utility, e.g. saying - "the LLM didn't write my paper, I just used it as a tool to read and summarize some research papers". But you didn't wield it to read those papers (as you might a Kindle). It read the papers, not you.

What do you miss by abdicating doing the reading? Pretty much everything. First and foremost, you miss learning how to write from those who can. You miss learning how to formulate an argument. You miss noticing things. You miss loading your background mind with fodder for novel ideas. You miss building trust in some authors and suspicion of others. You miss all the jokes. You miss all of the edges. You miss learning how to think.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Just say no to OpenAI and Anthropic
items.content:
I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in.

As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research.

Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages:

It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM)

You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below)

If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor

You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power

ChatGPT and Claude will never be private

These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do.

They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data?

OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers

Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed.

Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them.

Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program . To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it.

While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea.

I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. items.title: Linux May Get a New Home for AI Agent Skills
items.content:
A Fixes tag in a kernel patch points to the commit that introduced the bug, but the last commit to touch a buggy line may only have moved the code to a new file.

Sasha Levin, who co-maintains the stable and long-term support kernel trees, wants AI coding assistants to verify which commit introduced a bug before assigning it a Fixes: tag.

His two-patch series went to the workflows and ksummit mailing lists last week, where he has proposed a new agents directory in the kernel tree to hold the skill that does it.

The first patch adds an agents/ directory at the top of the kernel source tree for skills, prompts, and other resources meant for coding assistants. It also adds a MAINTAINERS entry covering the directory.

Each skill gets its own folder under agents/skills/ , with a SKILL.md file as its entry point, written in the Agent Skills format .

Assistants are told to read a resource directly from its path in the repository, and links inside a skill are relative to that skill's folder. A new section in the kernel's coding assistants document is meant to describe this layout.

The find-fixes skill, which arrives with the second patch, would be the first one in the directory.

Levin says the series traces back to a question from Ted Ts'o about incorrect tags in stable tree work. He pointed to LLM workflows that help find the right commit.

Ted later explained that the request came from a talk with Hannes Reinecke, who estimated that 15 to 20 percent of Fixes tags are wrong.

That matters beyond bookkeeping, since the tag is how stable maintainers and distributions work out which kernels need a given fix. A wrong one can send a fix to the wrong branches or leave a bug unpatched.

The new find-fixes skill reads Git history and returns a proposed tag with its evidence, while leaving the commit itself untouched.

The skill's guide.rst file says no single clue settles which commit a Fixes tag should name, not even an existing tag. The agent explains how the bug fails, traces candidate commits, and compares each against its parent.

It separates the commit that added the code, the one that made it defective, and any later change that only exposed the flaw.

For backported fixes, it checks whether the bug came from the original change or from how that change was adapted for an older kernel. Merges, reverts, and incomplete histories get their own handling.

When it cannot establish the origin, it returns no tag, lists the candidates and what is missing, and the fix stays a draft until someone resolves it.

The second patch would add a section to the kernel's coding assistants document saying an assistant must follow the guide before finalizing a bug fix or its commit message and when reviewing an existing tag.

The document's step for committing a fix would ask for a verified tag, where it now asks only for a Fixes tag. Keep in mind that the skill would not write commit messages, apply the tag, or decide whether a fix belongs in stable.

The series follows Levin's earlier push for the kernel's AI coding assistants policy, which we covered in April , and his proposal for a kernel killswitch .

Where the files should live is still open. The introductory patch message says he is unsure whether they belong under Documentation or in a separate agents directory at the root.

Greg Kroah-Hartman asked whether the series would fix tools skipping the kernel's guidance because an AGENTS.md file is missing. Sasha replied that this is a separate issue for the symlink patch.

items.content:
Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN.

Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent.

Is it different in incognito? Good. But it’s always the same? Bad news.

Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know you’re the … . I can use it to decide what ads you’ll see. But more importantly, if you’ve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AI…

Pretty soon I’d know more about you than your friends do - perhaps more than you know yourself.

“I have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevant… sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anyway…”

See, the thing is, it’s not about you at all. It’s not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, I’ll gladly take their money too.

I look at all this data and I don’t see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and it’s made of silicon! That’s the product.

What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer?

Remember the big fuss about third-party cookies? It was so big that the EU had already rolled out one of its greatest inventions - consent banners.

If EU ships faster than tech companies, that can only mean the tech companies are sitting on their hands. And one of those tech companies happens to hold two-thirds of the browser market.

Let’s give it up for Google - the biggest ad company on Earth!

ACT I. PRESSURE - “PRIVACY IS PARAMOUNT TO US, IN EVERYTHING WE DO.”

It’s 2019 and the cookies are still hot. It’s become bad PR and Safari and Firefox already block them.

A year later Google pledges: we will destroy cookies!! And establish a new, privacy-first reign.

ACT II. DISTRACTION - “INSTEAD OF DEPRECATING THIRD-PARTY COOKIES, WE WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW EXPERIENCE”

5 years later: people are now preoccupied with far greater worries than cookies, and the solutions Google has developed (Privacy Sandbox) kinda suck and have raised antitrust concerns so nobody uses them.

“You know what, let’s just keep the cookies. We’ll mask your IP address* though!” (* but only when incognito while authenticated) (** in the end they didn’t even deliver on that)

ACT III. ACCELERATION - YOU CAN NOW USE DEVICE FINGERPRINTING IN OUR AD PRODUCTS

Now there’s a better way to know who’s who!

The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a website’s code can’t see the data stored by other websites, and it can’t see your files or other applications without permission. Chrome and Edge stop here. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: A Modern Web App in C
items.content:
If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.

Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.

Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.

CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.

You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.

The stack is BCHS : OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.

There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.

There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.

There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.

There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.

Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.

OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.

libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.

libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.

libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.

Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.

libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.

SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.

Both are vendored and built as part of the project.

The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.

Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory.

CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.

There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:

If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.

It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.

A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.

CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.

It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.

In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).

With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.

I was mapping the OAuth flow that Google’s developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Google’s sign-in page. No account needed:

'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F'

The cookie is what caught my eye. Flask’s usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> , but about 1,200 bytes, way more than you need for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it.

Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed:

client_id = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com"

The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload, which was bad enough on its own. It also carried Google’s OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.)

I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs.

A client secret leaking in a cookie is a finding on its own. The part that mattered was that the same value verified the signature, so I nailed that down properly instead of trusting a lucky guess.

Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline:

derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b "cookie-session" , "sha1" )

I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take.

The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it:

items.title: Peppermint OS Expands Beyond Debian with Void Linux-Based PepVoid
items.content:
Peppermint OS , the lightweight Debian-based Linux distro, is expanding with PepVoid, an experimental edition built on Void Linux . The project announced a new round of testing, bringing updated ISO images and improvements ahead of a possible official release in November.

The initiative is very interesting because Void Linux takes a substantially different approach from Debian. Unlike Debian’s fixed-release model, Void follows a rolling-release approach, allowing users to receive software updates continuously without waiting for major upgrades.

Moreover, Void uses the XBPS package manager instead of APT and is a systemd-free distro, betting on the runit init system rather than systemd. These differences give PepVoid a distinctly different technical foundation while, at the same time, retaining the familiar Peppermint philosophy.

Importantly, PepVoid is not intended to replace the existing Debian-based Peppermint OS editions. Instead, the project explores an additional option for users interested in Void Linux while experimenting with improvements that could benefit its Debian-based offerings.

Peppermint OS brings its lightweight approach to Void Linux with PepVoid.

According to the developers, work on PepVoid began to bring the Peppermint approach to Void Linux’s rolling-release model. Initial testing images were made available earlier this year, and community feedback has helped guide further development.

The latest testing round introduces separate 64-bit ISO images, powered by Linux kernel 6.18, using either Xorg or XLibre. Both images are about 3.2 GB and are described as “PepVoid Loaded” builds, including a selection of preinstalled applications and utilities.

Another advantage is that PepVoid comes with the familiar Calamares graphical installer, making installation straightforward even for beginners. By comparison, standard Void Linux uses a CLI installation approach, making it better suited to experienced users.

The distro ships with an updated version of PepTools, Peppermint’s system utilities collection. The developers made adjustments for users who prefer graphical interfaces, making some system-management tasks more accessible without relying entirely on command-line tools.

As for software availability, PepVoid uses Void Linux’s standard upstream repositories, including the nonfree repository. The XLibre edition additionally includes a dedicated external repository maintained by the xlibre-void project to provide the necessary XLibre packages.

The developers also emphasize that the current selection of preinstalled software is not final. The team may add, remove, or change packages as testing continues and it evaluates community feedback.

Finally, the Peppermint OS team is targeting November 2026 for a possible official PepVoid release, though the timeline depends on testing progress and will coincide with planned ISO refreshes for the project’s Debian-based editions.

For now, users interested in trying the experimental edition can download the latest testing images from the project’s PepVoid download directory .

More information is available in the official announcement .

items.title: Docker Hub security advisory: personal access tokens transferred during account-to-organization conversions
items.content:
Docker Hub security advisory: personal access tokens transferred during account-to-organization conversions

On September 30, 2026, security researchers reported a vulnerability in Docker Hub’s identity and access management through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program. We confirmed the report and deployed a fix to production the same afternoon, less than four hours after receiving it. We then reviewed every account conversion back to the date the flaw was introduced, and on October 2, notified every user and organization owner whose account could have been impacted by this vulnerability. This post explains what the vulnerability was, what it could and could not do, what we found, and what we have changed.

We want to thank Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com for finding the issue, reporting it responsibly, and coordinating disclosure with us. Their technical write-up is available at ghostpat.com . This issue is tracked as CVE-2026-105445.

Was I or any member of my organization exposed to the vulnerability?

On October 2 at 5:30PM EST, we sent out an email with the subject line “Docker Hub Vulnerability Identified & Resolved” to the limited number of users exposed to this vulnerability. If you did not receive an email, you and any members of the organizations you administer were not exposed and there are no actions for you to take.

Docker Hub lets you convert a personal account into an organization. People do this because Hub has no way to move a repository from one account to another: conversion is how alice/app becomes an organization-owned alice/app without breaking every Docker pull that references it. During conversion, the user names an existing Docker Hub account as the new organization’s owner.

Beginning  August 26, 2024, conversion also re-assigned the converted account’s personal access tokens (PATs) to that new owner. It did this by changing the token’s owner record, without rotating or revoking the token secret. The named owner was not asked to confirm and was not notified. Together, those two gaps made the following possible:

An attacker creates an account and generates a PAT on it.

The attacker converts that account to an organization and names a target user as the owner.

The attacker’s PAT is re-assigned to the target user. The attacker still holds the secret and the PAT remains active now with the target user’s scope.

The token now authenticates to the registry as the target user.

Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access. Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.

The vulnerability did not give access to the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change the target’s password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over the account.

The exposure window ran from August 26, 2024, 20:33 UTC, until the fix was deployed on September 30, 2026, at approximately [19:10] UTC.

Sept 30, 11:40 AM: Report received at security@docker.com.

Sept 30, ~1:30 PM: We independently reproduced the issue with internal test accounts.

Sept 30, ~3:10 PM: Fix deployed to production and verified against the original proof of concept. Conversion no longer transfers PATs.

Sept 30, ~3:23 PM: Documentation updated to state that PATs do not transfer and must be recreated by the new owner, with organization access tokens recommended.

Sept 30, 4:59 PM: Researchers informed of the fix. Both parties agreed to coordinate disclosure.

Oct 2, 5:30 PM: Exposed users and their organization owners notified by email.

Oct 8, 3:45 PM: Forced deactivation of all PATs transferred through conversion, except where the account holder opted out.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

GlobalFoundries Returns to Advanced-Node Race With 7 nm-Class FDX Fusion
items.content:
GlobalFoundries Returns to Advanced-Node Race With 7 nm-Class FDX Fusion

Back in the now distant 2018, the semiconductor industry had three major players in contract leading-edge node manufacturing: TSMC, Samsung, and GlobalFoundries. At that time, Intel did not accept external clients. However, as node design became increasingly expensive—requiring multi-billion dollar investments—and more complex, with many players encountering yield and manufacturing difficulties, GlobalFoundries announced that it was stopping its 7 nm node development indefinitely. This left only two companies in the leading-edge race, but GlobalFoundries continued to develop unique semiconductor solutions that did not focus on smaller transistor sizes.

Today, the company is back at a similar stopping point but with a unique solution called FDX Fusion, based on fully-depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) technology. Unlike traditional CMOS, GlobalFoundries takes substrate isolation a step further by creating a fully insulating layer beneath the channel. This enables highly specialized capabilities, such as ultra-low-power in-memory computing, seamless integration of embedded non-volatile memory (like eMRAM), and highly efficient dense logic designs. With FDX Fusion, GlobalFoundries claims 7 nm-class node characteristics in terms of size and twice the transistor density of the first-generation 22FDX node, which was designated as a 22 nm-class design.

For manufacturing, GlobalFoundries plans to start FDX Fusion mass production in 2028 at its advanced facility in Dresden, Germany. This facility will be one of the strongest manufacturing regions in Europe, making chip sovereignty another important factor with the start of mass production. Customers can expect to receive initial technology demos next year, with PDK shipping in mid-2027. GlobalFoundries sees this node as a highly specialized solution for physical AI layers, applicable in areas from automotive and ASIC to the physical world, with sensing, heavy computations, and new requirements.
